# Installing Urbo

This page takes you from an empty Kubernetes cluster to a running Urbo: images, services, Keycloak,
secrets, values files, the Helm deployment, the first administrator and a smoke test. It follows
the way SWCode deploys the Urbo white label, so every step points at the file in this repository
it comes from. [Operating Urbo](README.md) describes the components;
[Configuration](configuration.md) lists the settings.

All hostnames here are placeholders: `app.example.org`, `cms.example.org`, `boards.example.org`,
`api.example.org`, `auth.example.org`, `search.example.org`, `images.example.org` and
`survey.example.org`.

## Before you start

### What you need

- **A Kubernetes cluster and Helm 3.** The workflows deploy with the `community-tooling/generic`
  chart from `https://community-tooling.github.io/charts/`.
- **An ingress controller and TLS certificates.** The values files are written for an nginx ingress
  (`kubernetes.io/ingress.class: nginx`) and cert-manager with a cluster issuer named
  `letsencrypt-prod`. Change these annotations to whatever your cluster uses.
- **A container registry** you can push to and the cluster can pull from.
- **The services** from [the component list](README.md#components): PostgreSQL, an S3-compatible
  object storage, Keycloak, MeiliSearch and imgproxy, plus whichever optional services you want.
- **A build host** with JDK 25, Node.js 24.16.0 and pnpm 11.5.3 (pinned in `app/.nvmrc` and
  `app/package.json`) and Docker. The backend build needs a GitHub token in `GITHUB_TOKEN` to pull
  packages ([backend README](../../backend/README.md#setting-up)); SWCode's release pipeline passes
  a packages-reader token the same way. The backend image downloads the OpenTelemetry Java agent
  from GitHub while it is built.
- **Outbound internet access from the backend** to the public data services, and to Brevo,
  Firebase and Instagram if you use them ([Configuration](configuration.md#external-data-sources)).

### Hostnames

Plan one public hostname, with a DNS record and a TLS certificate, for each of these:

| Placeholder | Serves | Ingress defined in |
|---|---|---|
| `app.example.org` | the citizen app | [`app/kubernetes/values-urbo.yaml`][app-values] |
| `cms.example.org` | the CMS | [`app/kubernetes/cms-values-urbo.yaml`][cms-values] |
| `boards.example.org` | urboards, if you run steles | [`app/kubernetes/urboards-values-prod.yml`][boards-values] |
| `api.example.org` | the backend API | [`backend/kubernetes/values-urbo.yaml`][backend-values] |
| `auth.example.org` | Keycloak | your Keycloak deployment |
| `search.example.org` | MeiliSearch, for the citizen app's and urboards' searches | your MeiliSearch deployment |
| `images.example.org` | imgproxy | your imgproxy deployment |
| your S3 endpoint | the bucket's objects | your object storage |
| `survey.example.org` | LimeSurvey, if you use surveys | your LimeSurvey deployment |

The object URLs the backend hands out are virtual-hosted style by default
(`https://<bucket>.<endpoint host>/<key>`), so the bucket's own hostname has to resolve and carry a
valid certificate, unless you switch to path style ([Storage](configuration.md#storage)).

## Build the images

### Which source to build

Build from a stable tag of the public mirror: `backend-vX.Y.Z` for the backend and `app-vX.Y.Z` for
the frontends. The two trains are versioned independently, but the CMS and the backend keep no
compatibility window for each other: while only one of them is updated, the CMS's permission
screens do not work
([ADR-015](../architecture/arc42/09-architecture-decisions.md#adr-015-the-backend-defines-access-levels-and-their-presentation)).
Deploy both from releases of the same time.

### How SWCode's pipeline builds them

For reference, this is what the release workflows do:

- **Backend.** On an rc tag, Gradle builds the jar with `bootJar -PappVersion=<version>`, and Docker
  builds [`backend/Dockerfile`][backend-df] with `backend/` as context. The image is tagged
  `latest` and with the version from the tag, without its `backend-v` prefix.
- **Frontends.** On an rc tag, `pnpm run ci:build` builds the whole workspace once in `app/`. Then
  one Docker build per image, each with `app/` as context: [`app/Dockerfile`][app-df] for the
  citizen app, [`app/Dockerfile.urboards`][boards-df] for urboards and
  [`app/apps/cms/Dockerfile`][cms-df] for the CMS. Each image is tagged `latest` and with the
  version.
- **Stable tags build no image.** They only publish the Maven and npm packages; the stable release
  runs the image of the rc it was cut from. rc tags and rc images older than 14 days are deleted,
  except the newest rc and the rcs that a stable tag shares its commit with
  ([Versioning](../versioning.md)).
- The images go to `ghcr.io/sw-code/urbo/<name>`, and the backend's values files pull them with an
  image pull secret named `image-pull-secret`.

### Building them yourself

The backend image copies a jar that you build first:

```bash
cd backend
GITHUB_TOKEN=<token> ./gradlew bootJar -PappVersion=<version>
cd ..
docker build -t registry.example.org/urbo/urbo-cms-backend:<version> backend
```

The frontend images copy a build that you make first. Their configuration (API URL, Keycloak, search
key, map, analytics) is compiled into the build, so set it in the `environment.prod.ts` files before
you build ([Frontend build configuration](configuration.md#frontend-build-configuration)). Build in
a full checkout: `pnpm install` runs the `prepare` script, which generates the API clients from the
backend's OpenAPI files under `backend/`.

```bash
cd app
pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
URBO_RELEASE_VERSION=<version> pnpm run ci:build
cd ..
docker build -f app/Dockerfile -t registry.example.org/urbo/urbo-web-app:<version> app
docker build -f app/Dockerfile.urboards -t registry.example.org/urbo/urboards:<version> app
docker build -f app/apps/cms/Dockerfile -t registry.example.org/urbo/urbo-cms-frontend:<version> app
```

`URBO_RELEASE_VERSION` pins the version stamped into the build; the release workflow sets it to the
tag's version. If you move the build output between machines before the Docker build, keep its
hidden directories: the citizen app's `.well-known/` (app links) is one.
